text: My dad's reading glasses are still on the kitchen windowsill. Nobody moves them. Every morning I make coffee next to them and pretend it is a normal thing to do, standing beside a pair of glasses that are waiting for a face that is not coming back.

We sat on the bus stop bench for forty minutes and talked about everything except the one thing. You said you were fine. I said I was fine. The bus came twice and we let it go both times, which I think was the most honest thing either of us did all night.

The library had a staircase that went down further than the building did. I counted one hundred and twelve steps before I stopped counting. At the bottom was a reading room with no windows and a single lamp, and someone had left a book open to a page that described exactly where I was standing.

When the power grid failed for the third week, our block started a theater. We performed on the roof at sunset because it was the only light we had. Mrs. Okafor played every queen. Nobody asked why we were doing it. Everyone came anyway, with blankets and whatever food they could spare.

1. The color of your jacket the day you left. 2. I bought the same one. 3. I do not wear it. 4. It hangs in my closet like a question. 5. Some days I open the door just to check that it is still blue.

This morning a heron stood in the creek behind the parking lot for eleven minutes without moving. I was late for work and I watched the whole thing. When it finally lifted off, slow and enormous, I said thank you out loud to nobody, and I meant it.

I worked at the same hotel front desk for twenty-two years. I was proud of never letting a guest see me upset. It was only after I retired that I realized I had also never let my wife see it, or my son, or, for the most part, myself.

The cashier asked to see my receipt and did not ask the woman behind me. It took four seconds. I have replayed those four seconds more times than I have replayed my graduation, and I am tired of how small it was and how large it stays.

The church in our town had one stained glass window, and the light from it landed on the third pew at exactly ten in the morning. My grandmother sat there every Sunday for fifty years. When they sold the building, I drove four hours to sit there one more time.

The river flooded the lower market again, the third time this year. By noon the fishmongers had moved their tables up the hill and the tricycle drivers were ferrying old people for free. Nobody organized it. We have just learned that the water is not going to wait for anyone to organize anything.

I have shelved books at the university library for thirty-one years. No student has ever learned my name. But I know which ones come back every Thursday for the same poetry anthology, and I have started leaving it on the cart where they can find it.

At the hospice, the kids drew pictures for the patients. Mine went to a man named Roberto who drew one back for me: a house with too many windows and a sun in the corner wearing sunglasses. He died on a Tuesday. I still have the sun.

I moved to a city where nobody knew my family so I could finally be the person I was in my head. The first night, a stranger smiled at me across a bar and I left before my drink arrived, because it turns out you bring your hometown with you in your shoulders.

After she died, I made spreadsheets. Insurance numbers, funeral costs, the dates her prescriptions would have needed refilling. My brother said it was unhealthy. I told him it was the only thing in the house that still added up.

Walking down Fifth at noon, I am thinking about lunch, and then about my mother's hands, and then about a song from 2009, and then about whether the man selling hot dogs is happy, and then the light changes and I have lived an entire small life between two curbs.

I wanted to be the mayor's chief of staff by thirty. I made it by twenty-nine. The first thing I learned was that every decision costs someone a park or a bus route, and the second thing I learned was that I had stopped asking who.

My lola talked to her tomato plants every morning. She thanked them before she picked anything. As a kid I thought it was a joke. Now I have my own balcony garden in Queens and I catch myself saying salamat to a basil plant, completely serious.

My sister and I lived in eight apartments in six years, always near water: a harbor, a canal, a lake that smelled like rust. We never unpacked the second box. When she finally moved out, she left her half of the box behind, still taped.

I have spent four summers on a boat trying to photograph one particular whale that a fisherman swore he saw. My friends think I have lost it. Maybe. But every time the water goes still, I feel like something enormous is looking back at me from underneath.

The exchange program put me in a village where it snowed nine months a year and nobody used my name, only the word for foreigner. In the spring a neighbor finally invited me in for tea. We sat in silence for an hour and I think it was the warmest conversation of my life.

I keep a notebook of every stranger who has mistaken me for someone else. Forty-three so far. Sometimes I wonder if one of those people is the real me and I am just the one who happened to get the body.

She lived in the house with the gate and I lived in the apartment above the bakery. At school we were best friends. On weekends I never invited her over, and I told myself it was because the stairs were steep.

After the funeral I started running the trail behind the reservoir at five in the morning. There is a fox that crosses the path near the second bridge. Some days it stops and looks at me, and for a second neither of us is pretending anything.

The nurse wrote down my pain as a four even though I said eight. I watched her pen move. I said nothing because I was tired and because I have learned which rooms will not hear me no matter how loud I say it.

My childhood house is a parking lot now. I looked it up on the map. There is a blue car parked exactly where my bedroom used to be, and I find, to my surprise, that I am glad someone is using the space.

I painted my bedroom the exact shade of the sweater you wore the night you said you did not love me anymore. My therapist asked why. I told her I wanted to understand the color, as if a color could explain anything.

In the evacuation center, a kid started drumming on an empty water jug. Within ten minutes there were eight of us, and an old man was singing a song in a dialect I did not know. For one hour nobody was waiting for anything.

My grandmother taught me that you can pray with your eyes. You just look at something long enough and carefully enough, a mango, a cloud, your own hand, and eventually the looking becomes a kind of thank you.

I want to be clear that I was a good brother. I drove him to every appointment that year. If I sometimes left him in the parking lot to finish my phone calls, that was only because the calls were important, which I am sure he understood.

My father was a pastor who did not believe in God for the last ten years of his life. He told me this on a fishing trip, quietly, like he was handing me a set of keys. Then he went back to preaching every Sunday, and I never asked him how.
Since the accident, time comes in strange lengths. A Tuesday afternoon can last a year. Then I look up and it is March. The doctor calls it normal. I call it living in a clock that someone dropped.

We got married at twenty-three with big plans: a bookstore, a dog, a house in the province. Ten years later we have the dog. Last night we sat on the floor of our apartment and admitted that the dog was the only plan we had ever really wanted.

At the clinic they asked me to check male or female, and I sat with the pen above the paper for so long that the receptionist came over to help. I wanted to tell her it was not a hard question. It was just the wrong one.

The elder showed us which roots to leave in the ground so the plant would come back next year. Take half, she said, and then thank it for the half you took. I wrote it in my notebook and then realized it was not a note about plants.

I can tell you the exact minute the call came: 3:17 a.m. I can tell you the brand of the hospital coffee and the number of tiles on the waiting room ceiling, eighty-four. I cannot tell you a single thing anybody said to me that night.

My roommate thought I was quiet because I was shy. Really I was doing the math on every dinner invitation, whether I could afford it, whether I could afford to say no. By spring she had stopped asking, and I was too relieved to be sad about it.

I work the overnight shift at a hospital that is three buildings joined by tunnels. At 4 a.m. I sometimes take the long way just to walk the empty corridors, where the lights hum and every door looks like it could open onto a different century.

When the factory closed, the church basement became a job center, a food bank, and a daycare in the same month. The priest learned to use spreadsheets. Nobody called it a miracle, but nobody had a better word for it either.

My dog is fourteen and cannot climb the stairs anymore, so I moved my mattress to the living room. We sleep side by side on the floor. Every night I listen to her breathe and memorize the sound, just in case memory works the way I hope it does.

In Manila I was a disappointment. In Madrid nobody knew enough about me to be disappointed. I lived there for two years, happy and slightly ashamed of how happy I was, like I had stolen a coat from a stranger and it fit.

My mother wanted to be an architect. Instead she drew floor plans for other people's houses on the back of receipts at the sari-sari store she ran for thirty years. I found a box of them after she retired. Some of them were beautiful.

We scattered his ashes in the bay, and the wind blew half of them back onto the boat. Nobody knew what to do. Finally my aunt started laughing, and then we were all laughing, and that is the part of the day I remember best.

My grandfather's hands were scarred from the cane fields. He never talked about it. When I was ten I traced the scars with my finger while he slept, like a map of a country nobody had ever bothered to draw.
After the earthquake our school had no roof, so the music teacher held class in the basketball court. We learned one song all semester. It was not a very good song. I still know every word.

There is a single tree in the courtyard of my dorm. I have decided it is mine. I know when its leaves turn, which branch the pigeons prefer, and the exact afternoon in April when it suddenly remembers how to be green.
